opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that division is really modeled on how a human research lab actually works. In the Virtual Lab, the human researcher works with an AI principal investigator agent, and that PI agent assembles a team of AI scientist agents, each with its own expertise. In our nanobody project, for example, we had an immunologist, a machine learning specialist, and a computational biologist, plus a scientific critic agent.

The group meetings are where the big-picture decisions get made. The PI sets an agenda, often with questions the human researcher has given it. Then the agents go around in several rounds, each giving their perspective from their own expertise. The critic pushes back, pointing out weaknesses or things that are underspecified. At the end, the PI synthesizes the discussion into a decision. That's how we chose the overall strategy, like whether to design nanobodies or antibodies, whether to start from existing nanobodies and mutate them, and which computational tools to use, such as ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta. Those are questions that really benefit from multiple viewpoints, the same way a real lab meeting does.

The one-on-one meetings are for executing specific tasks. Once the team has decided on a plan, an individual agent, say the ML specialist, meets one-on-one with the PI or the critic to actually do the work, like writing the code to run ESM scoring or to process the AlphaFold outputs. That's much more focused. You don't need five agents debating how to parse a PDB file. Usually the critic gives feedback on the code or the approach, and the agent iterates.

One thing we found useful is running the same meeting multiple times in parallel, often with higher temperature, and then holding a merge meeting where the PI consolidates the best ideas across those runs. It's a bit like getting several independent opinions and then synthesizing them, and it makes the outputs more robust.

Throughout all of this, the human stays in the loop but intervenes pretty sparingly. In the nanobody work, the agents did the vast majority of the talking, and the human mainly provided high-level guidance and agendas. So it's group meetings for strategy and breadth, and one-on-ones for depth and implementation.

r001.rationale: It says group meetings are where big-picture decisions and the overall research strategy are decided.

r002.rationale: It describes one-on-one meetings as focused on executing specific tasks, such as writing code and processing outputs.

r003.rationale: It describes the critic pushing back on group discussions and giving feedback on work in one-on-one meetings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the design choices we thought hardest about, and it ended up mirroring how real research labs work more than we initially expected.

In the Virtual Lab, you have a PI agent, and then a team of scientist agents with different expertise, so for the nanobody project that was an immunologist, a computational biologist, a machine learning specialist, and then a scientific critic whose whole job is to push back. And the work gets split into two kinds of meetings.

The team meetings are for the high-level, strategic decisions. What's the overall approach going to be? Should we design nanobodies de novo or should we modify existing ones? Which tools should we even consider using? Those are questions where you genuinely want multiple perspectives colliding, because the immunologist is going to care about different things than the ML person, and the critic is going to poke holes in both. So the PI poses the agenda, each agent gives their view, the critic weighs in, and this goes for a few rounds until the PI synthesizes a decision. The value there is really in the disagreement and the diversity.

The individual meetings are for the actual execution. Once the team has decided, okay, we're going to use ESM for the mutation proposals and AlphaFold-Multimer for structure evaluation, somebody has to actually go write that code. And you don't want five agents in a room trying to write a Python script together, that's just noise. So the PI meets one-on-one with, say, the computational biologist, gives them a very specific task, and that agent produces the deliverable. The critic is often still in those individual meetings to review the output, catch bugs, point out where the code doesn't match the spec.

So the rough heuristic is: team meetings for decisions that benefit from breadth, individual meetings for tasks that benefit from focus. And honestly, that's exactly how I run my own lab. You don't bring the whole group together to debug one person's code, but you do bring everybody together when you're choosing a direction.

One thing that surprised us a bit is how much the quality improves when you let the team meetings run for multiple rounds and when you run them in parallel and then merge. Having the PI see several independent discussions of the same question and then consolidate turned out to be a pretty cheap way to get more robust decisions. It's a little like asking the lab the same question on different days and noticing what's consistent.

r001.rationale: It says team meetings handle high-level strategic decisions, including choosing the project’s overall approach and tools.

r002.rationale: It describes one-on-one meetings as the place to assign and execute specific tasks, such as writing code.

r003.rationale: The critic pushes back in team meetings and is described as often joining individual meetings, but the response does not clearly establish that the critic provides feedback across all Virtual Lab meetings.

astra-6.text:
We use group meetings for questions where you want the different scientists to bring their expertise together—for example, deciding on the overall research direction or discussing how to approach a problem. The PI leads that discussion, and the other agents contribute from their respective perspectives.

Once there’s a concrete task, we can assign it to an individual scientist in a one-on-one meeting. That gives them space to work through the details without involving the whole team. Then we bring those results back into a group meeting to discuss them and decide what to do next. So there’s an alternation between collective discussion and focused individual work.

r001.rationale: It says group meetings are used to decide the overall research direction.

r002.rationale: It says concrete tasks are assigned to individual scientists to work through in one-on-one meetings.

r003.rationale: It does not identify a critic agent or say that one provides constructive feedback across meetings.

sol-6.1.text:
We use group meetings for the big-picture decisions, where it’s helpful to have the different agents bring their perspectives together. So, for example, defining the research question, deciding on an overall strategy, or discussing results and what to do next. The AI principal investigator leads that discussion and synthesizes the input from the other scientists.

Then the one-on-one meetings are for more focused work. The principal investigator can work with an individual scientist on a particular task, like developing a computational method or writing code. That lets them go deeper without having the whole team involved in every detail. They can then bring those results back to a group meeting, so you alternate between coordination across the team and specialized work.

r001.rationale: The response says group meetings handle big-picture decisions, including defining the research question and choosing an overall strategy.

r002.rationale: The response says one-on-one meetings focus on an individual scientist’s specific task, such as developing a method or writing code.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a critic agent or say that one provides constructive feedback across meetings.
